```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      out.width = "100%")
```

```{r setup}
library(OncoCohortSelect)
```

Three single-arm cohorts are run in parallel: Cohort1 receives the reference
regimen and Cohort2 and Cohort3 receive new regimens. At the end of the trial
one cohort is selected for further development. Cohort1 is the default, and a
new regimen is selected only if the data favor it. This article compares
decision rules based on the posterior benefit-risk score and on win statistics
by their selection probabilities in simulated trials.

## What makes a rule better

The statistics of the two approaches are on different scales, so their raw
values cannot be compared. A fair comparison fixes, for every rule, the
probability of selecting a new regimen when none is better than the reference
(here, three identical cohorts), and then compares the probabilities of
selecting the right cohort when a new regimen is better. The right cohort of
each scenario must be fixed before the simulation and independently of the
rules: by scenarios in which one cohort is at least as good as the others on
every endpoint, and, for trade-offs between efficacy and safety, by the
choice the clinical team would make if it knew the true parameters.

## Scenarios

Each scenario gives the true PFS and OS medians, response rates and adverse
event rates of the three cohorts. In the last scenario Cohort3 is the most
active but has an adverse event rate of 0.45, which the clinical team is
assumed to have judged unacceptable, so the right choice is Cohort2.

```{r}
make_arm <- function(pfs, orr, os) {
  CorOncoEndpoints::OncoArm(pfs.median = pfs, orr = orr, resp.cor = 0.4,
                            death.prop = 0.15, os.median = os)
}
ref_arm <- make_arm(5, 0.30, 14)
mid_arm <- make_arm(7, 0.45, 17)
top_arm <- make_arm(8.5, 0.55, 19)
scenarios <- list(
  "Null" = list(arms = list(Cohort1 = ref_arm, Cohort2 = ref_arm, Cohort3 = ref_arm),
                ae = c(0.20, 0.20, 0.20)),
  "Cohort2 better" = list(arms = list(Cohort1 = ref_arm, Cohort2 = mid_arm,
                                      Cohort3 = ref_arm), ae = c(0.20, 0.20, 0.20)),
  "Cohort3 best" = list(arms = list(Cohort1 = ref_arm, Cohort2 = mid_arm,
                                    Cohort3 = top_arm), ae = c(0.20, 0.20, 0.20)),
  "Cohort3 toxic" = list(arms = list(Cohort1 = ref_arm, Cohort2 = mid_arm,
                                     Cohort3 = top_arm), ae = c(0.20, 0.20, 0.45)))
right <- c("Null" = "Cohort1", "Cohort2 better" = "Cohort2",
           "Cohort3 best" = "Cohort3", "Cohort3 toxic" = "Cohort2")
nsim <- 100
```

The number of simulated trials is kept small so that the article builds
quickly; with 100 trials a probability of 0.5 has a Monte Carlo standard error
of 0.05, and an evaluation would use several thousand trials.

## Rules

Four rules are compared. In each trial, the new cohorts whose statistic
exceeds a threshold are candidates, and the candidate with the largest
statistic is selected; without a candidate, Cohort1 is selected.

* `br_diff`: the benefit-risk score against target values minus that of
  Cohort1. The cohorts must also be admissible: the posterior probability that
  the adverse event rate is at most 0.4 must be at least 0.8.
* `br_ref`: the benefit-risk score relative to Cohort1, with the same kind of
  admissibility condition on the difference of the adverse event rates.
* `ntb` and `wr`: the net treatment benefit and the win ratio against Cohort1,
  with priority OS, PFS, response and adverse event.

```{r}
eps <- list(
  Endpoint("OS", "tte", time = "os_tte", event = "os_event"),
  Endpoint("PFS", "tte", time = "pfs_tte", event = "pfs_event"),
  Endpoint("ORR", "binary", var = "response"),
  Endpoint("AE", "binary", var = "ae", higher.better = FALSE))
crit <- data.frame(endpoint = c("ORR", "PFS", "OS", "AE"),
                   target = c(0.30, 0.50, 0.60, 0.40), time = c(NA, 6, 12, NA),
                   weight = c(1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1), cutoff = c(NA, NA, NA, 0.8))
crit_ref <- data.frame(endpoint = c("ORR", "PFS", "OS", "AE"),
                       measure = c("rate", "hr", "hr", "rate"),
                       target = c(0.10, 0.80, 0.90, 0.10),
                       weight = c(1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1 / 3, 1), cutoff = c(NA, NA, NA, 0.8))
```

Each scenario is simulated with 40 patients per cohort, enrolled over 12
months and analyzed at month 24. `SimSelection()` returns one row per trial
and cohort with all the statistics.

```{r}
res <- lapply(seq_along(scenarios), function(i) {
  sc <- scenarios[[i]]
  d <- SimCohorts(nsim = nsim, n = c(40, 40, 40), arms = sc$arms, ae.rate = sc$ae,
                  cutoff = 24, a.time = c(0, 12), seed = i)
  SimSelection(d, eps, crit, reference = "Cohort1", criteria.ref = crit_ref)
})
names(res) <- names(scenarios)
head(res[["Cohort3 best"]][, c("sim", "group", "br", "adm", "br_diff", "br_ref", "ntb",
                               "wr")])
```

`plot()` shows the distribution of a statistic over the simulated trials for
each cohort, here the net treatment benefit against Cohort1 in the scenario
"Cohort3 best".

```{r}
plot(res[["Cohort3 best"]], "ntb")
```

The pairwise comparisons use the scoring rule of Gehan; `scoring = "peron"`
in `SimSelection()` uses the rule of Péron instead.

## Calibrated thresholds

The thresholds are chosen in the null scenario so that a new cohort is
selected in at most 10% of the trials.

```{r}
stats <- c("br_diff", "br_ref", "ntb", "wr")
thr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(stats, function(s) {
  CalibrateThreshold(res[["Null"]], s, alpha = 0.10)
}))
thr
thr_ntb <- thr$threshold[thr$statistic == "ntb"]
```

In the null scenario, a new cohort is selected by the net treatment benefit
when its value lies above the dashed line, the calibrated threshold.

```{r}
plot(res[["Null"]], "ntb", threshold = thr_ntb)
```

## Selection probabilities

```{r}
oc_row <- function(r, s, th) {
  oc <- SelectionOC(r, s, threshold = th)
  p <- stats::setNames(oc$p_select, oc$group)
  out <- c(p[c("Cohort1", "Cohort2", "Cohort3")], "(none)" = 0)
  if ("(none)" %in% names(p)) out[["(none)"]] <- p[["(none)"]]
  out
}
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(res), function(sc) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(stats), function(i) {
    data.frame(scenario = sc, rule = stats[i],
               t(oc_row(res[[sc]], stats[i], thr$threshold[i])), check.names = FALSE)
  }))
}))
tab$right <- mapply(function(i, g) tab[[g]][i], seq_len(nrow(tab)), right[tab$scenario])
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
             caption = "Probability of selecting each cohort at the calibrated thresholds")
```

The column `right` is the probability of selecting the right cohort of the
scenario. In the scenario "Cohort3 best", the rules select Cohort3 with
probabilities between
`r round(min(tab$right[tab$scenario == "Cohort3 best"]), 2)` and
`r round(max(tab$right[tab$scenario == "Cohort3 best"]), 2)`. In the scenario
"Cohort3 toxic", they select Cohort2 with probabilities between
`r round(min(tab$right[tab$scenario == "Cohort3 toxic"]), 2)` and
`r round(max(tab$right[tab$scenario == "Cohort3 toxic"]), 2)`, and Cohort3
with probabilities between
`r round(min(tab$Cohort3[tab$scenario == "Cohort3 toxic"]), 2)` and
`r round(max(tab$Cohort3[tab$scenario == "Cohort3 toxic"]), 2)`. The
admissibility condition of the benefit-risk rules excludes a cohort with too
many adverse events, whereas in the pairwise comparisons the adverse event has
the lowest priority and decides only the pairs left undecided by OS, PFS and
response; a rule based on win statistics gives more weight to safety when the
adverse event comes earlier in the priority order.

With several thresholds, `SelectionOC()` shows how the selection
probabilities change with the threshold; the dashed line is the calibrated
threshold of the net treatment benefit.

```{r}
oc <- SelectionOC(res[["Cohort3 best"]], "ntb", threshold = seq(0, 0.4, by = 0.02))
plot(oc, threshold = thr_ntb)
```

## Saturation of the score against target values

In the scenario "Cohort3 best", the median scores against the target values
are

```{r}
r3 <- res[["Cohort3 best"]]
round(tapply(r3$br, r3$group, median), 3)
```

The score measures how certainly a cohort exceeds the targets, not by how
much. When several cohorts clearly exceed the targets, their scores approach 1
and the differences carry little information; the score relative to the
reference cohort and the win statistics compare the cohorts directly.

https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.3923

Chakraborty, S., Dubey, A. K., Kumar, A. and Chan, I. (2026). A two-stage dose
optimization framework for oncology drug development with multiple efficacy
and safety endpoints via an integrated benefit-risk assessment. *Statistics in

https://doi.org/10.1080/19466315.2026.2668381
